A.question: What NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommendations or clinical trial evidence address targeted therapy for EGFR alterations in cancer? Cite the specific guideline or trial.
A.text:
1315", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching published medical literature, guidelines, FDA, CDC, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}], "done": true, "summary": "Analyzed query, searched for evidence"}


EGFR-targeted therapy is established primarily in non–[small cell lung cancer](/rare-disease/small-cell-lung-cancer) (NSCLC), where NCCN, ASCO, and ESMO guidelines converge on EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs)—osimertinib above all—across the metastatic, resected, and unresectable stage III settings, with mutation-specific regimens for exon 20 insertions and antibody-based combinations. The strongest guideline-shaping trials are FLAURA, FLAURA2, MARIPOSA, ADAURA, LAURA, and PAPILLON. The recommendation depends heavily on mutation subtype (classical exon 19 deletion/L858R vs. exon 20 insertion vs. uncommon mutations) and disease stage, so the evidence is organized below by those axes.
First-line metastatic disease — classical mutations (exon 19 deletion / L858R)
NCCN lists three preferred category 1 first-line options: osimertinib monotherapy, osimertinib plus carboplatin/cisplatin and pemetrexed (nonsquamous), and lazertinib plus amivantamab.[[1]] ASCO guidelines recommend offering osimertinib with platinum-pemetrexed or amivantamab plus lazertinib, with osimertinib monotherapy retained for patients declining combination therapy.[[2]] The supporting trials:
- FLAURA established osimertinib over first-generation TKIs (gefitinib/erlotinib), with median PFS 18.9 vs. 10.2 months (HR 0.46) and median OS 38.6 vs. 31.8 months (HR 0.80, P=0.046).[[3]][[4]]
- FLAURA2 showed osimertinib plus platinum-pemetrexed improved median PFS to 25.5 vs. 16.7 months (HR 0.62) and OS 47.5 vs. 37.6 months (HR 0.77, P=0.02), with a pronounced benefit in CNS-metastasis patients but higher grade ≥3 toxicity (64% vs. 27%).[[2]][[5]][[6]]
- MARIPOSA showed amivantamab plus lazertinib improved median PFS vs. osimertinib (23.7–27.5 vs. 16.5–18.5 months; HR 0.68) at the cost of more infusion reactions, cutaneous toxicity, paronychia, and VTE.[[7]][[8]][[9]]
The ASCO first-line EGFR treatment algorithm summarizes these pathways:
[[10]]
Here is the NCCN first-line algorithm for exon 19 deletion / L858R disease:
[[1]]
Uncommon mutations (S768I, L861Q, G719X)
NCCN recommends afatinib, erlotinib, dacomitinib, gefitinib, or osimertinib first-line, with osimertinib or datopotamab deruxtecan as subsequent therapy.[[1]] These alterations (~10% of EGFR-mutant NSCLC) respond to certain TKIs such as osimertinib and afatinib on a mutation-specific basis.[[1]]
Exon 20 insertion mutations
These are generally resistant to classical EGFR TKIs and require dedicated agents.[[1]] NCCN lists carboplatin/pemetrexed plus amivantamab (nonsquamous, category 1, preferred) as the only first-line option, with amivantamab, sunvozertinib, or datopotamab deruxtecan as subsequent therapy.[[1]] ASCO guidelines recommend first-line sunvozertinib monotherapy or platinum doublet plus amivantamab.[[2]] Key trials:
- PAPILLON — amivantamab added to carboplatin-pemetrexed improved PFS vs. chemotherapy alone (HR 0.40; ORR 73% vs. 47%).[[2]]
- WU-KONG28 — first-line sunvozertinib improved median PFS vs. chemotherapy (10.3 vs. 7.5 months; HR 0.65).[[2]]
- In the previously treated setting, ASCO guidelines offer amivantamab or sunvozertinib after platinum chemotherapy (CHRYSALIS ORR 40%; WU-KONG6/WU-KONG1B supporting sunvozertinib). Mobocertinib was withdrawn after failing its phase 3 endpoint.[[2]][[11]][[12]]
The NCCN exon 20 insertion algorithm:
[[1]]
Second-line / resistance setting (classical mutations)
After progression on osimertinib, NCCN and ASCO recommend amivantamab plus carboplatin/pemetrexed (MARIPOSA-2: median PFS 6.3 vs. 4.2 months, HR 0.48).[[1]][[2]][[7]] Datopotamab deruxtecan is an option after both an EGFR TKI and platinum chemotherapy (pooled TROPION-Lung-01/05 ORR 45%)[[2]].[[1]] For progression on first/second-generation TKIs with T790M, osimertinib is indicated.[[1]][[2]] The COMPEL study supports continuing osimertinib with chemotherapy in selected non-CNS progressors.[[2]]
Adjuvant therapy (resected disease)
NCCN recommends adjuvant osimertinib for resected stage IB–IIIA (and IIIB T3–T4, N2) EGFR exon 19 deletion/L858R NSCLC, category 1 when given after or instead of platinum chemotherapy.[[1]] ASCO (stage III guideline) recommends adjuvant osimertinib after platinum-based chemotherapy (evidence strength high).[[13]] This rests on ADAURA: disease-free survival HR 0.17–0.23 for stage II–IIIA and a significant OS benefit (HR 0.49, 5-year OS 85% vs. 73%).[[13]][[14]][[15]] A Cochrane meta-analysis found a pooled OS HR of 0.54 for adjuvant EGFR TKIs, driven largely by ADAURA.[[16]][[17]]
Unresectable stage III disease
For stage III EGFR exon 19 deletion/L858R NSCLC that has not progressed after definitive chemoradiation, NCCN recommends consolidation osimertinib (category 1), rather than durvalumab.[[1]][[11]] This is based on the LAURA trial, which showed a PFS benefit for consolidation osimertinib.[[4]][[18]]
Other cancers
The retrieved evidence is overwhelmingly NSCLC-centric; no guideline recommendations for EGFR-activating-mutation–directed TKI therapy in other solid tumors were identified in these results. (EGFR-targeting antibodies such as cetuximab/panitumumab in colorectal cancer act on wild-type EGFR pathway status rather than activating EGFR mutations and are a distinct topic.)

B.question: What NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommendations or clinical trial evidence address targeted therapy for EGFR alterations in cancer? Cite the specific guideline or trial.
B.text: 6d32", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching published medical literature, guidelines, FDA, CDC, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}, {"callid": "728bb162-1484-4eeb-922e-c834bb3c0f17", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching full-text sources from NEJM, JAMA, Nature, NCCN, Cochrane, Wiley, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}], "done": true, "summary": "Analyzed query, searched for evidence"} EGFR-directed targeted therapy is guideline-established almost entirely in NSCLC harboring activating EGFR kinase-domain mutations, where NCCN and ASCO recommendations now span first-line metastatic, post-progression, adjuvant, and stage III consolidation settings.[[1]][[2]][[3]] Outside NSCLC, the anti-EGFR antibodies cetuximab and panitumumab are used in colorectal cancer based on RAS/BRAF status and primary tumor sidedness rather than on any EGFR alteration, and[[4]][[5]] EGFR amplification/EGFRvIII in glioblastoma has no guideline-recommended targeted therapy despite ~40 trials.[[6]][[7]] Metastatic NSCLC with exon 19 deletion or L858R — first line The NCCN NSCLC guideline (NSCL-21) lists three preferred category 1 options: osimertinib, (carboplatin or cisplatin)/osimertinib/pemetrexed (nonsquamous), and lazertinib + amivantamab-vmjw. Afatinib, dacomitinib, erlotinib, erlotinib + bevacizumab, erlotinib + ramucirumab, gefitinib, and lazertinib are listed as useful in certain circumstances.[[2]] Note that dacomitinib has been permanently discontinued in the US by the manufacturer, with no safety or efficacy concern cited.[[8]] ASCO guidelines recommend clinicians offer osimertinib with platinum-pemetrexed or amivantamab plus lazertinib (Recommendation 1.1; moderate evidence, strong recommendation), with osimertinib monotherapy for patients not pursuing combination therapy (Recommendation 1.2).[[1]] [[1]][[9]][[10]][[11]] No head-to-head comparison of the two combinations exists; an indirect comparison found no significant PFS (HR 0.79) or OS (HR 0.95) difference, with toxicity profile driving selection.[[12]] Amivantamab-specific prophylaxis is mandatory and is written into the NCCN algorithm: prophylactic anticoagulation at initiation to prevent VTE; oral doxycycline or minocycline, clindamycin lotion to the scalp, chlorhexidine to nails, and a ceramide-based non-comedogenic moisturizer for dermatologic toxicity; and oral dexamethasone 8 mg for 2 days before the first dose to reduce infusion-related reactions.[[2]] Progression on osimertinib (classical mutations) NCCN NSCL-22 branches by pattern of progression: asymptomatic or oligoprogressive disease (trials included up to 3–5 sites) → definitive local therapy (SABR, surgery, or SRS for brain) with continuation of the TKI; multiple progressing lesions → carboplatin/pemetrexed + amivantamab-vmjw (category 1, preferred, nonsquamous, if not previously given), or lazertinib + amivantamab-vmjw (useful in certain circumstances, if not previously given), or other systemic therapy. Neither amivantamab-containing option applies to S768I, L861Q, or G719X tumors.[[2]] Biopsy at progression is advised to exclude small cell transformation (~6%) and to define resistance mechanisms.[[2]] Datopotamab deruxtecan-dlnk is listed as preferred subsequent therapy for EGFR-mutant disease, with FDA approval restricted to patients who have received prior EGFR-directed ther[[2]]apy and platinum chemotherapy.[[8]] ASCO Recommendation 2.1 is platinum-based chemotherapy with amivantamab, based on MARIPOSA-2 (median PFS by BICR 6.3 vs 4.2 months, HR 0.48; ORR 64% vs 36%; intracranial PFS 12.5 vs 8.3 months), with substantially more toxicity — treatment interruption 65% vs 33%, discontinuation 18% vs 4%, VTE 10% vs 5%.[[1]] PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy is less effective in EGFR-mutant NSCLC irrespective of PD-L1 expression.[[2]] For patients progressing on a first- or second-generation TKI, repeat biomarker testing should be performed and T790M-positive disease treated with osimertinib (median PFS 10.1 vs 4.4 months versus platinum-pemetrexed, HR 0.30; ORR 71% vs 31%)[[1]].[[2]] Exon 20 insertions NCCN NSCL-25 gives carboplatin/pemetrexed + amivantamab-vmjw (nonsquamous) as category 1 preferred first-line therapy, with amivantamab-vmjw or sunvozertinib as subsequent therapy (each only if not previously received).[[2]] ASCO Recommendation 1.6 is sunvozertinib monotherapy or platinum doublet plus amivantamab:[[1]] - PAPILLON: amivantamab + carboplatin-pemetrexed vs chemotherapy — PFS HR 0.40, ORR 73% vs 47%; neutropenia 59%, paronychia 56%, rash 54%.[[1]] - WU-KONG28 (phase III, first line): sunvozertinib median PFS 10.3 vs 7.5 months (HR 0.65), ORR 58.9% vs 31.1%; grade 3 CK elevation 20.9%, diarrhea 14.1%.[[1]][[13]] - After platinum, ASCO Recommendation 2.7 permits amivantamab (CHRYSALIS ORR 40%) or sunvozertinib (WU-KONG6 ORR 61%; WU-KONG1B ORR ~46–47% at 200 and 300 mg, with ILD reported as a serious AE in 5%).[[1]] Mobocertinib was withdrawn after failing its phase III primary endpoint.[[8]] Testing caveat: PCR-based assays under-detect exon 20 insertions, so NGS is preferred, and the specific insertion matters — p.A763Y764insFQEA is TKI-sensitive and insLQEA may be sensitive to first- and third-generation TKIs.[[2]] Atypical mutations (G719X, S768I, L861Q) NCCN NSCL-24 lists afatinib or osimertinib as preferred, with dacomitinib, erlotinib, and gefitinib as other recommended first-line options.[[2]] ASCO offers afatinib (Recommendation 1.3; ACHILLES showed PFS HR 0.422 and ORR 61.4% vs 47.1% versus platinum doublet), amivantamab plus lazertinib (1.4; weak/weak — CHRYSALIS-2 cohort C ORR 52%, treatment-naive PFS 19.5 months), and osimertinib (1.5; UNICORN ORR 55%, PFS 9.4 months) — all excluding exon 20 insertions and T790M.[[1]] Structure-function classification increasingly guides selection: L861Q behaves as classical-like and favors osimertinib, whereas G719X and S768I are PACC mutations with more consistent afatinib activity.[[13]][[14]] Resected and unresectable stage III disease - ADAURA: 3 years of adjuvant osimertinib 80 mg daily after complete resection of stage IB–IIIA ex19del/L858R NSCLC — DFS HR 0.23 in stage II–IIIA (4-year DFS 70% vs 29%), OS HR 0.49 (5-year OS 85% vs 73%), CNS DFS HR 0.24. An exploratory 8-year landmark update reported OS HR 0.52 for stage IB–IIIA (8-year OS 79% vs 64%). ASCO guidelines recommend adjuvant osimertinib after platinum-[[3]][[15]][[16]][[17]]based chemotherapy in resected stage III disease (high evidence, strong recommendation) — osimertinib does not replace indicated chemotherapy. - LAURA: osimertinib after definitive chemoradiotherapy in unresectable stage III ex19del/L858R NSCLC — median PFS 39.1 vs 5.6 months (HR 0.16); grade ≥3 AEs 35% vs 12%, radiation pneumonitis 48% vs 38%; second interim OS HR 0.67 (31% maturity). NCCN makes osimertinib the category 1 consolidation choice in this population and explicitly excludes durvalumab for ex19del/L858R tumors, warning of toxicity when a TKI is given in temporal proximity to immunotherapy. POLESTAR showed a comparable result with aumolertinib (PFS 30.4 vs 3.8 months, HR 0.20).[[2]][[3]][[18]][[19]][[20]] Other tumor types - Colorectal cancer: ASCO guidelines recommend anti-EGFR therapy plus doublet chemotherapy first-line for MSS/pMMR left-sided RAS wild-type mCRC, explicitly not for right-sided or RAS-mutant disease, and not with triplet chemotherapy (left-sided OS HR 0.71 vs chemotherapy-bevacizumab; right-sided HR 1.35). NCCN mirrors this in COL-D[[4]][[5]]. BRAF V600E is not a blanket exclusion from anti-EGFR antibodies: encorafenib + cetuximab or panitumumab, with or without chemotherapy, is NCCN-preferred in that subgroup. Selection is driven by RAS/BRAF/MMR status and sidedness — not by an EGFR alteration. - Glioblastoma: EGFR alterations occur in up to 57% and EGFRvIII in ~11%, but TKIs, monoclonal antibodies, and the ADC depatuxizumab mafodotin have all failed to show benefit (randomized phase II depatux-m HR 1.04), attributed to limited BBB penetration, subclonal heterogeneity, and ecDNA dynamics. Brain-penetrant agents (silevertinib/BDTX-1535, ERAS-801) and intraventricular EGFRvIII CAR-T rem[[6]][[21]]ain investigational. Would you like to explore how to choose between osimertinib-chemotherapy and amivantamab-lazertinib based on CNS disease, TP53 status, and ctDNA?
